canberra.title: Cyclist, 57, dies in Federal Highway crash with car
canberra.snippet: Police are investigating the fatal crash that occurred when a cyclist and a car collided in northern Canberra on Thursday afternoon (19 N...
canberra.content:
19 November 2026

A cyclist died in a fatal crash with a car on the Federal Highway on Thursday afternoon (19 November). Photo: ACT Policing.

Police are investigating the fatal crash that occurred when a cyclist and a car collided in northern Canberra on Thursday afternoon (19 November).

An ACT Policing spokesperson said a car and cyclist collided on the Federal Highway near the Horse Park Drive off-ramp around 1 pm.

The 57-year-old male cyclist died at the scene.

“The driver of the vehicle, a 19-year-old woman, was transported to hospital by ACT Ambulance Service paramedics for observations,” the police spokesperson said.

The cyclist is the 13th person to die on ACT roads this year.

The northbound lanes of the Federal Highway were closed, and diversions were put in place for a time after the crash.

“ACT Policing’s Major Collision Team are investigating the circumstances of the collision,” the police spokesperson said.

If you saw the crash, or have dashcam footage of it, contact Crime Stoppers ACT. Quote P2506053.

canberra.title: Hackett community shocked at three-storey supportive housing proposal
canberra.snippet: The first Hackett residents knew about a three-storey public housing project being built in the middle of their suburb was when the devel...
canberra.content:
An artist’s impression of the Hackett public housing proposal. It’s too big, residents say. Image: Our Architect.

The first Hackett residents knew about a three-storey public housing project being built in the middle of their suburb was when the development application sign appeared two weeks ago.

With only a week until the representation period on the proposal ends, residents are preparing for a community meeting near the site on Friday (20 November) to see what can be done about it.

But the short notice and a Territory Priority Project declaration make that a tall order.

Welcome to Planning Minister Chris Steel’s new world order in which “nimby” (his word) opposition to vital public housing is given short shrift

The $6.6 million supportive housing proposal is for two blocks, one the site of the former ESA depot and the other a treed bit of green space next to Hackett Oval

The combined 3631 sqm site at 4 Holtze Close is zoned Community Facilities (CFZ).

The three-storey, 14-metre-high building, which will sit on a one-level, 33-space basement carpark, will comprise nine one-bedroom, 15 two-bedroom and three three-bedroom units. A single-storey waste enclosure and a new substation are also included.

Eleven of the 15 trees on the site are regulated. Five pinus radiata and three of the regulated trees will need to go, but nine new trees will be planted.

Residents are dismayed by the lack of notice and consultation, and say the building is too big and out of character with the suburb’s low-rise houses.

Spokesperson Liam Jones said it would likely be the biggest building in Hackett if approved.

Mr Jones said it would be a massive change to the area that no one’s talked to residents about.

“It feels a little bit like they’ve hidden it from the community deliberately,” he said.

“They’ve been working on this for many months, potentially up to a year to get it to this stage, and they have not talked to anyone in the community.

“They’re hiding behind the regulations to enable them to get sign-off on this project and push it through. I just don’t think that’s really a respectful way to engage with the community.”

There were concerns about a public housing project of this size being built next to the well-used oval, close to a school and child care centre.

Mr Jones said similar public housing in nearby Watson had been accompanied by an increase in crime.

He said the Hackett community was inclusive and was open to a conversation about more community housing in the suburb, but not at this scale.

Forcing a lot of at-risk and vulnerable people to live in massive public housing developments was not fair to the community or to the tenants.

“You see much better outcomes where people are given enough space for independence, and that is happening across the city,” he said.

“Are they going to put in extra services in this location to support these people?

“Are they gonna put in a concierge-type arrangement to support these people and help them with any issues, as we see in other locations?”

Mr Jones said residents would be pushing for the DA to be paused until the community could decide whether it was comfortable with the scale of what’s proposed.

He said the design, the number of storeys, the tree loss and the encroachment on green space were also issues.

Residents were being urged to make a submission and contact MLAs.

Mr Jones was scathing about the government’s approach of springing this on the community without any discussion and trying to railroad development wherever it liked.

“The culture in the ACT Government is that they don’t talk to communities about it,” he said.

“That needs to be fixed. That is a fundamentally disrespectful way to govern.”

Mr Steel made his position clear in annual report hearings this week and at the Property Council’s Housing Summit.

“There’s a recognition that maybe we shouldn’t be allowing nimby groups to systemically and unfairly target public and community housing developments through appeals to ACAT,” he told the Housing Summit.

Mr Steel told a hearing that he intended to streamline the system even further so housing projects wouldn’t be “unfairly held up” in ACAT processes.

He said there were many projects to come, with seven community and public housing TPPs under assessment.

The residents’ meeting, facilitated by the Hackett Community Association, will take place at 5 pm near the site.

The representation period for the Hackett DA closes on 25 November.

canberra.title: Unemployment rate jumps sharply to a five-year high of 4.9 per cent
canberra.snippet: Unemployment has jumped sharply to 4.9 per cent, sparking attacks on the Federal Government’s handling of the economy, and calls fo...
canberra.content:
About 43,500 jobs were shed in October, and the unemployment rate jumped to 4.9 per cent. Photo: Julia Gomina.

Unemployment has jumped sharply to 4.9 per cent, sparking attacks on the Federal Government’s handling of the economy, and calls for the Reserve Bank of Australia not to impose another interest rate hike.

The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose to 4.9 per cent in October, up from 4.7 per cent in September, according to the latest data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

It is the highest unemployment rate since October 2021.

The RBA has suggested that an unemployment rate between 4.5 per cent and 5 per cent would be needed to bring down inflation.

About 43,500 jobs were shed over the month, while the participation rate fell by 0.2 of a per cent.

ABS head of labour statistics, Sean Crick, said in October there were 44,000 fewer employed people and 18,000 more unemployed people.

“Similar to last month, we had a higher proportion of people remaining unemployed than we would usually see in October in the post-Covid era,” he said.

“The youth unemployment rate – that is, for people aged between 15 and 24 – increased to 11.3 per cent in October from 11.1 per cent in September.

“This is the highest it’s been since October 2021. In the post-Covid period (from May 2022 onwards), the youth unemployment rate has averaged 9.2 per cent.

“Employment remained steady in trend terms, meaning there was very little underlying growth in the number of employed people.

“The employment-to-population ratio fell 0.3 percentage points to 63.3 per cent, and the participation rate fell 0.2 percentage points to 66.6 per cent.”

The number of hours worked fell 0.2 per cent in October, and the underemployment rate fell 0.1 percentage points to 6.2 per cent.

The Federal Government said the latest jobs figures continue to reflect the impact of higher interest rates and ongoing global uncertainty, including conflict in the Middle East.

“These figures show the very real and serious pressure that Australians are under right now,” Treasurer Jim Chalmers said.

“Given higher interest rates and the challenges coming at us from around the world, it’s unsurprising to see unemployment tick up, but that doesn’t make it any less of a concern to Australians.

“While the labour market eased in October, our unemployment rate remains relatively low and that reflects the resilience of Australia’s economy.

“We’ll continue to do what we can to help Australians with the cost of living, support more jobs and address inflation.”

Employment Minister Amanda Rishworth said that, despite softening over the month, the participation rate remained high at 66.6 per cent and there are now 83,500 more Australians in work than a year ago.

The Coalition is laying the blame squarely at the feet of the Federal Government for the rise in the jobless rate.

Deputy Opposition Leader Jane Hume said Labor had lost control of the economy.

“Anthony Albanese’s economy is not working for Australians. Australians have found themselves not better off. They are poorer under Labor,” Senator Hume said.

“More businesses are going under and more Australians are finding themselves out of work.

“So to those 43,500 people that are now unemployed this month that weren’t last month, why don’t we ask them whether Anthony Albanese’s commitment came true?

“He said before the 2022 election that Australians would be better off under Labor.”

The Australian Council of Social Service has called for restraint over interest rate hikes.

ACOSS chief executive officer Cassandra Goldie said since interest rates started to rise in 2022, around a quarter of a million people have been pushed out of paid work.

“We have been warning for some time that interest rate hikes would lead to devastating human consequences,” Dr Goldie said.

“Unemployment is projected by the RBA to rise to 5.1 per cent by the end of 2028, but at this point that forecast looks quite optimistic. Australia is staring down a materially sharper downturn and, at worst, a recession … To protect people’s living standards, the RBA and government must coordinate. The RBA should refrain from further increases to rates, with their interest rate rises still working their way through the economy and likely to further increase unemployment.”

The ACTU has also demanded an end to interest rate increases, saying the latest rise in the unemployment rate means the RBA has already cooled the economy and lifting interest rates again next month would put more jobs at risk.

“So many people are just one expense away from keeping their heads above water, and the Reserve Bank should look through its inflation-taming obsession to see the workers who are hanging on by a thread,” ACTU secretary Melissa Donnelly said.

canberra.title: Integrity Commissioner accuses DPP, police of passing the buck on potential Kingfisher prosecution
canberra.snippet: The ACT Integrity Commissioner has issued a scathing response to police opting not to pursue criminal charges relating to Operation Kingf...
canberra.content:
ACTIC Commissioner Michael Adams (right) with ACTIC CEO Judy Lind doesn’t believe referral for prosecution in needed in regards to Operation Kingfisher findings. Photo: Screenshot.

The ACT Integrity Commissioner has issued a scathing response to police opting not to pursue criminal charges relating to Operation Kingfisher and expects no movement from the prosecutor’s office either.

ACT Chief Police Officer Scott Lee previously told annual reports hearings he was concerned that, because some evidence in the report was obtained through “compellable” means, it had implications for any possible criminal charges or prosecution.

ACTIC Commissioner Michael Adams wasn’t impressed with the stance.

“All this says is ‘I don’t want to do this, go to the DPP [Director of Public Prosecution]’,” he said.

“And I suspect the DPP will say ‘oh, I don’t want to do this, go to the Chief Police Officer’.”

As for the reasoning that compulsorily obtained material isn’t admissible for prosecution, Mr Adams said police had other tools that their disposal.

“Whether there is evidence that could be used for the purposes of charging is an entirely different question,” he said.

“And that would be answered by a careful reading of the report, because a great deal of the evidence I refer to … was not compulsorily obtained.

“Or, if it were compulsorily obtained, can be admitted because it could be obtained by other methods than those under the Integrity Commission Act.

“There is evidence that can’t be used, but whether there’s other evidence that can be used, whether, in the end, it amounts to enough, is another [matter].”

The Operation Kingfisher report outlined former Education Directorate head Katy Haire’s serious corrupt conduct could constitute offences under the ACT’s Criminal Code.

These included general dishonesty, conspiracy to defraud, knowingly giving false or misleading information, producing false or misleading documents and abuse of public office.

The Integrity Commission also determined former Education Minister chief of staff Joshua Cermadis could be open to charges relating to conspiracy to defraud and abuse of public office.

Mr Adams was asked whether he felt the police or DPP should be looking at pursuing criminal charges or prosecution.

“No-one’s sought my advice,” he said.

Mr Adams stated both agencies had their own protocols and discretion to follow.

The Integrity Commission Act 2018 means the Commissioner cannot recommend prosecution for potential criminal offences outlined in an investigation report.

The key word is “recommend”, as that suggests giving an opinion.

The DPP’s office has previously pointed to section 111 of the Act, which does allow for the formal referral of matters.

ACT DPP Victoria Engel SC said that was the only way her office could consider the report’s contents.

“I understand the Commissioner made it plain [in his hearing] that that referral has not been made,” she said.

Ms Engel took Mr Adams’ comments to mean he had chosen to make the report public rather than make a referral – which she said was consistent with her experience in other jurisdictions.

She added there was always a risk to potential prosecution if findings were made public (as they were in this case).

“We have communicated to [Mr Adams] that, given there’s no section 111 referral … we will liaise with police if they intend to pursue the matter,” Ms Engel said.

“I await a referral, if that is to come.”

Shadow Attorney General Chiaka Barry questioned if the functionality or effectiveness of the ACTIC was undermined if, when serious corrupt conduct findings were made, no prosecution was sought.

Ms Engel questioned that assertion.

“[The ACTIC has] different roles, including public awareness, public reporting and raising issues in a public domain,” she said.

“[No prosecution] is not uncommon – this goes to one of the other functions of the Integrity Commission of calling out this conduct, laying it bare for the community to see so it’s not repeated in the future.

“It doesn’t always result in prosecutor action.”

Ms Barry commented that usually, when it’s suspected a crime has occurred, an investigation and potential charges will follow.

“But in this case, where public officials should be held to a higher standard, it seems not to be common process for criminal charges to actually be considered,” she said.

australia.title: Australian music industry rejects ‘divide and conquer’ proposal to give musicians exemption from AI scraping
australia.snippet: Reported proposal to give musicians special treatment is ‘unworkable’, Aria CEO says, vowing to stand with other creatives Get our daily ...
australia.content:
The music industry will not accept an AI carveout deal that leaves other creative sectors behind, rejecting a reported proposal to give musicians special treatment while allowing big tech to train on other copyrighted material – described by David Pocock as a “divide and conquer strategy”.

The trade union representing writers and creatives is “alarmed” at a proposal to let AI companies train on Australian data if they buy a permit, an idea also strongly rebuffed by the Coalition and Greens.

The Albanese government would not comment on the reported proposal, but senior ministers have raised concerns about current copyright law in recent days, hinting reforms were needed.

Annabelle Herd, the CEO of the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria), and Claire Pullen, the CEO of the Australian Writers’ Guild, said the creative community – which this week launched a major AI campaign – would remain united in rejecting such changes.

“I can’t see any creative workers leaving their colleagues behind,” Pullen said.

The Australian Financial Review reported on Thursday the government was considering a copyright change under which AI companies would buy permits to train on Australian content, but that music may be exempted. Such a proposal would be more in line with AI companies, after Anthropic suggested a model of “conditional approval” to scrape content unless a rightsholder objected, and OpenAI told a parliamentary committee it would “potentially” support paying into a fund for creators.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Guardian Australia was not able to independently verify details of the proposal. One senior member of the creative community, involved in copyright discussions with government, said they had heard some details of such an idea, but others said they had not and doubted the Albanese government would seriously entertain it. One source in the AI industry, who declined to be named, said they would welcome such a plan.

Herd said she was unaware of the proposal before Thursday, but the music industry would not desert other creatives.

“Had we been consulted, we would have advised this scheme is unnecessary, unworkable and designed to suit the commercial interests of AI companies, not protect creators,” she told Guardian Australia.

“Our position is unchanged: we stand with the rest of the creative and media industries.”

Herd and Pullen said such a scheme would be difficult to implement technically, questioning how content like movies or TV shows – which combine copyrighted elements such as music, video and screenwriting – would be treated if just one element was exempted from AI scraping.

“This just seems like such a convoluted path, when AI companies have had an open invitation to sit down and negotiate for years. We have been working with government to come up with a model since 2024. We’ve come up with solutions and tech has steadfastly refused to even talk,” Pullen said.

While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has declared it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, and that artists “need to be compensated”, some AI companies have argued it is too difficult to make individual licensing deals under existing copyright law.

The Media, Entertainment & Arts Alliance said it would be “alarmed” at the reported proposal, and demanded protections promised by Albanese “must apply to all creative sectors”.

While government MPs declined to comment on the report, senior Labor figures have recently begun more forcefully pointing to what they claim are shortfalls in copyright law in the AI age – despite major rightsholder groups rejecting the need for change. The industry minister, Tim Ayres, on Tuesday said “the status quo is no good” for creative workers, a line repeated by the acting prime minister, Richard Marles, on Thursday. Marles added on News24: “People are being ripped off”.

The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, also used newly strengthened language when contacted, promising “certainty and strong protections for Australian artists”.

“Right now, the work of Australian creatives is being used without their consent or payment,” a spokesperson for Rowland said.

“The Government has long advocated for tech companies to strike commercial deals with Australian artists, and we will continue to do so.”

Potentially carving out musicians did not win support among parliamentarians, either.

The shadow attorney general, Michaelia Cash, claimed such a proposal would “divide the rightsholders”.

“This ham-fisted tactic should be strongly resisted. Everyone who owns property should have the same right for it not to be stolen.”

Pocock also described it as “some sort of divide and conquer strategy”.

“It’s hard to know what [Labor] are actually doing at the moment. The joint select committee hasn’t even given its report to the government, and we’re hearing all sorts of whispers about what the government is planning.”

Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young urged the government not to meet copyright demands requested by big tech.

“What they’re asking Australia to do actually is to undermine copyright the world over. Australia will become known as the Cayman Islands for AI if we allow this loophole to happen,” she told News24.

“I say, don’t be that stupid. Stand up to them.”

australia.title: An elevator, a brick wall and a bathroom: scientists use gravity to send ‘practically unblockable’ message
australia.snippet: Australian physicists chose to transmit the word ‘gravity’ in binary code through brick wall Get our breaking news email , free app or da...
australia.content:
Australian scientists have used gravity as a means of communication, in a proof-of-concept experiment involving a snail-paced 1950s elevator, a brick wall and a men’s bathroom.

Physicists at the University of Queensland have used gravity to transmit a “practically unblockable” message about 70cm through a brick wall, by sending an elevator up and down between two floors and measuring changes in the gravitational field as a result of the movement.

The research, published in the journal Science Advances, involved a sensitive detection device known as a gravimeter, which was set up on the floor of a men’s bathroom adjacent to the lift.

The gravimeter was able to detect the position of the elevator’s 1.8-tonne counterweight as it moved between two levels – representing 0 and 1 in binary code – which enabled the scientists to send a message.

The researchers chose to transmit the word “gravity”, or 1000111 1110010 1100001 1110110 1101001 1110100 1111001 in binary code. At a transmission rate of one bit (digit) per minute, the single word took nearly an hour to send.

The scientists say that while gravitational communication is currently far from usable given its extremely slow speed, an advantage is that it is a “practically unblockable wireless communication scheme”.

“Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” said co-author Dr Charles Woffinden, of UQ’s school of mathematics and physics, in a statement. “Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with wifi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.”

Study co-author Prof Matthew Davis told Guardian Australia: “At the moment, it’s very hard to imagine how it could be practically useful.” But he added that the experiment was “theoretically interesting enough that it was worth doing”.

To put into perspective how slow the message transmission was, Davis said that Nasa’s Voyager 1 spacecraft, which after 49 years of travel had just reached a distance of one light-day away, could “communicate with Earth at a faster data rate than our communication concept”.

According to Davis, the new method of communicating could theoretically occur at ranges of up to 500 metres and at a rate 15 times faster, if more sensitive quantum gravity sensors were used.

The idea for the elevator study arose from a project to develop a contactless weighbridge – which would use quantum sensors to detect changes in the strength of gravity due to a passing truck, allowing scientists to determine the mass of a large vehicle.

Classical gravimeters can be thought of as a mass on a spring. “If you stretch the spring, the mass bounces up and down at a certain rate, which is determined by the spring and the gravitational field,” Davis said. “If the gravitational field changes ever so slightly, the rate at which it bounces back and forth changes.”

“Quantum sensors are still under development,” Davis said.

“Sometimes doing physics leads in unexpected ways and it’s a bit of fun … you get to do quirky things on the side,” he added. “It’s one of the great joys of science to have stuff like this happen.”

Other near-unblockable methods of communication – involving neutrinos or gravitational waves – have been proposed, “but these approaches are somewhat hindered by the difficulty in generating a measurable signal”, the scientists note.

The physicists conducted the research in UQ’s Parnell physics building, which is also home to the world’s longest-running science experiment – the pitch drop experiment, which began in 1927.

australia.title: Coalition fight emerges as Taylor urged to ‘stand up’ to Nationals on EU free trade deal
australia.snippet: Matt Canavan has attempted to block the deal before a formal Coalition decision is reached, leaving some Liberals fearing they are being ...
australia.content:
A split is emerging in the Coalition as multiple Liberals privately call for the opposition to negotiate with Labor to support the EU free trade agreement, with some fearing they were being wedged by the Nationals.

The deal has faced stiff opposition from the Nationals whose leader labelled it “the worst deal ever”, as well from some farmers over export levels for agricultural products and a climate clause binding Australia to meet its obligations under the Paris agreement.

Guardian Australia spoke to six Liberal MPs and senators who raised concerns that Matt Canavan’s attempt to block the trade deal before a formal Coalition decision had been reached had backed the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, into a corner.

Several Liberals, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said the Coalition was the party of free trade agreements, and that wholly opposing the deal would “not be a good sign” for a party of government.

One Liberal MP said the party needed to “stop pandering to the Nationals”.

“They are destroying our reputation in the cities by their pandering to the dark vested interests that sustain them,” they said.

“Gus must stand up and be strong for our values and economic common sense. Otherwise his leadership will be questioned.”

A second, who also asked not to be named, said a group of MPs, largely moderates, were “a bit incensed” by Canavan’s intervention and that the party should “hold their nose” and support the agreement, while negotiating for additional domestic provisions for farmers.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

They said the Nationals leading the public debate before the issue had been discussed internally was the “tail wagging the dog”, but that this would not result in a “Sussan-esque fall out” and that the relationship between Taylor and Canavan was still solid.

The former cabinet minister Alex Hawke said the US midterms were an important reminder for the Nationals that protectionist policies did not win votes.

“It’s not a perfect agreement, but I am on the side of letting the government sign the agreement,” he said, adding that to vote against it would be against the national interest.

“I would like Matt Canavan and the Nationals to have a bigger think about the impact of protectionism and tariffs and the catastrophe it’s caused for the global economy.”

The outspoken Liberal senator Andrew McLachlan, who has flagged voting in favour of the agreement, said there were “still many real Liberals in the party room that believe the EU trade deal should be supported”.

“Being a traditional Liberal and one that has consulted on the EU agreement in my state, I see no merit in any of the arguments that suggest that we should oppose the deal,” he said.

A third MP said most Coalition members did not actually understand the agreement, which would be examined in detail by the treaties committee next year.

“Most party room members have no idea what’s in the FTA and keep reading about it in the newspapers,” they said.

Regional voices now ‘louder’ than in the past

They estimated roughly half the party room would support the agreement with caveats such as more money for farmers and clarity on climate provisions.

But they noted that unlike other free trade agreement negotiations, the Coalition now largely consisted of regional MPs representing those regional and agricultural industries, “therefore the voices on the ag side are much louder than they’ve previously been”.

A senior Liberal backed in this view.

“Since we came into opposition, the Nationals have been expanding their reach and control over the Coalition’s messaging, and every leader has to wrestle with it – Dutton, Sussan, and now Angus,” they said.

“We’re hoping Angus will understand that free trade is in the DNA of the Liberal party and we need to have a strong position on this.”

Five other Liberals disagreed with the “perception” that Taylor had been wedged.

One said it was “entirely appropriate” that the leader of a party committed to agricultural regions would lead the debate.

“Particularly the [deal’s] constraints on Australia’s governance on climate would be unacceptable to most voters,” they said.

“The economy is everything that matters and any conditions that would be detrimental needs to be debated.”

The MP said given the party room rejected net zero just over 12 months ago, raising concerns about the cost of policies is legitimate.

After almost a decade of negotiations, Labor hammered out a deal with the bloc in March, expected to be worth $10bn a year.

The deal contains a commitment to respect the Paris climate agreement, which Australia is already a signatory to.

The shadow foreign minister, Ted O’Brien, has asked Labor to push for a letter from Europe clarifying that as long as Australia remains a signatory to Paris any future government will maintain sovereignty to make other climate policy changes.

Labor, which holds 30 seats in the Senate and needs nine more to reach a majority, says it could cobble together a “Frankenstein” agreement with crossbenchers and renegade Liberals to pass legislation in the upper house. It could also secure the support of the Greens.

There is no single bill for the deal, but smaller pieces of legislation that need to be passed to implement the agreement.

The trade minister, Don Farrell, said his door was “always open” to parliamentarians.

“My aim is that every single vote is in favour of this deal, which is crucial for Australia’s future,” he said.

Taylor has previously said Labor would be in breach of the trade agreement “almost immediately” as the government wasn’t on track to meet its own climate targets.

australia.title: ‘Communities are really angry’: how Australia’s datacentre opposition has gone from marginal to mainstream in five months
australia.snippet: A network of grassroots campaigners around the country are sharing information to help push back against the datacentre boom Get our brea...
australia.content:
When Heather Champion raised a council motion in March opposing a massive new gas plant to power a large datacentre in the Southern Highlands of New South Wales, it failed to pass.

Five months later, when the local councillor for Wingecaribee raised a new motion calling for the federal government to implement a moratorium on new datacentres, it passed unanimously.

“I think the council’s change in perspective is a direct result of the change in sentiment in the community,” Champion says.

The shift highlights grassroots successes in pushing back on datacentre construction and how those wins are inspiring other communities to take similar action.

In May, Guardian Australia reported on three datacentre projects across the country – Hazelmere in Western Australia, West Footscray in Victoria, and Lane Cove in New South Wales.

Since the report, the project proposals have been withdrawn in WA and NSW, and NextDC’s M3 expansion in West Footscray has been stalled after Jemena, the power provider, delayed the installation of taller power poles after the community outcry.

Lane Cove Responsible Planning spokesperson, Sasha Titchkosky, says after the success of having the Goodman Group’s Mars datacentre in Lane Cove withdrawn, she is working with communities in western Sydney and the Southern Highlands on their own campaigns.

Titchkosky says by working together, the groups send a strong signal to industry and politicians that they need to do better.

As it stands, councils play a role in approving datacentres in some states, but in others, such as NSW and Victoria, fast-tracked approvals skip the local council stage. The federal government has proposed rules that would from next year set mandatory minimum requirements for large datacentres, including how projects manage energy, water, costs, community engagement, location and workforce impacts.

“Just saying they’re going to put in place regulations, but still allowing datacentres to be approved … isn’t good enough.

“They [need to] either put a pause on approvals or basically say that everyone who gets approved now will be subject to the regulations when they come in force.”

Campaigners across Australia are sharing notes and tips through WhatsApp, using the platform to organise rallies and discuss new proposals.

In Victoria, a community wiki site displays a map of locations of datacentre proposals, the community groups organising around them, and links to campaign tips from US groups that successfully lobbied against the sector in the recent midterm elections.

Titchkosky has been in contact with campaigners in the Southern Highlands, where an application refusal for one of three gas plants capable of producing 673MW of power in total is being challenged in the NSW land and environment court. The applicant, Cloud Carrier, wants to use the gas plant to power a “data campus” in Moss Vale with AI “at its core”.

“We’ve been in touch with Lane Cove for quite a long time.

“We are sharing skills, messages – it’s very lateral and it’s very informal,” Champion says of the community networks’ organic growth.

They share what works and what doesn’t work – and what might work in one area may not be suitable in another, she says.

“[Lane Cove’s] circumstances are just so completely different but in some ways that’s been really helpful … having [our] voices combined does provide some breadth.”

The groups are also working with communities in western Sydney to build their capacity to take on new centres planned for the area.

Mandy Ottaviano, a masters of sustainability student at the University of Sydney who has been researching community action against datacentres in Australia says there is a “real desire” for the groups to connect with each other, but there is no formal organisation.

“What we’re not seeing a lot of yet is [non-government organisations] stepping in and bridging that gap in terms of coordinating those groups in a meaningful way together,” she says.

“We haven’t yet seen any emergence of a national kind of coalition.”

The chief executive officer for Data Centres Australia, Belinda Dennett, acknowledges there is “more interest from the community” in datacentre development than ever before, and datacentre companies are stepping up community consultation.

“This ranges from community information sessions, door knocking, newsletters, websites, hotline phone numbers and social media updates,” Dennett says.

“Third parties delivering energy, broadband and water infrastructure are also an important part of building community support so we also encourage more coordination and information sharing between parties.”

Mixed messages

While state and federal governments appear to be reacting to the growing community concerns over datacentres – some states are introducing new rules and the federal government is set to follow suit early next year – campaigners are concerned the changes don’t go far enough.

The New South Wales parliament’s long-running inquiry into datacentres released its report earlier this month, with the committee voting to remove two contentious recommendations: that the NSW government advocates for a moratorium on new datacentre developments until new obligations are in place; and to advocate for the new federal rules to be applied retrospectively.

The chair, Greens MP Abigail Boyd, was the only committee member to vote in support of the recommendations.

“It appears that both the Labor and Liberal parties remain in hock to the industry talking points,” Boyd said in the chair’s foreword in the report.

“I was particularly disappointed that both Labor and Liberal parties voted together against a pause on data centre approvals until sufficiently robust and legally binding obligations are in place, and similarly voted against advocating for data centres currently in the planning pipeline to have to comply with any rules that are currently being contemplated.”

Boyd said the delay to the rules coming in federally “makes clear the coordinated effort by governments and industry to avoid having to comply with even the most moderate of environmental and social obligations”.

Champion says she was “really frustrated” the recommendations were removed.

“We agreed between the group of us we would call for a moratorium, and all the community groups know that’s what’s needed.

“It feels like a real cop-out to be honest.”

Titchkosky says it is “clear as day where the two major parties” sit on datacentres – and questions whether the move may prove politically destructive, given datacentre disquiet played a pivotal role in voter sentiment in the US midterms.

“They’re ultimately prepared to sell out communities for multinational corporate interests,” she says. “I think we are going to see the same issues play out in Victoria and NSW in our upcoming elections as they were in the US midterms.

“Communities are really angry about this.”

australia.title: Mark Speakman resigns and says Liberals face ‘existential threat’ as NSW exodus continues
australia.snippet: Former NSW opposition leader warns party against becoming ‘Labor lite’ or ‘One Nation lite’ in late-night speech Get our breaking news em...
australia.content:
Former New South Wales opposition leader, Mark Speakman, will not contest his seat at the March state election, the latest in a mass exodus of MPs under the Liberal leader who replaced him, Kellie Sloane.

In a late-night speech on Thursday, the final sitting day of NSW’s legislative assembly ahead of the vote, Speakman said he would not contest his south Sydney seat of Cronulla, which he has held since 2011.

He is the eighth out of 24 current Liberal MPs to announce they will not re-contest their seat in March, following Jordan Lane, Mark Coure, Tanya Davies, Ray Williams, James Griffin, Mark Taylor and Alister Henskens.

The announcement comes almost a year to the day after Speakman resigned from the leadership of the opposition in a spill in favour of Sloane, who was elected unopposed.

In that time the Coalition has gone from commanding 28% of the primary vote in New South Wales to 23%, Sydney Morning Herald Resolve polling suggests.

Labor has gone from 37% to 30%, while One Nation, which Resolve did not start polling separately until March, is currently at 26%.

Last week, Sloane said her party would not form government with One Nation, but she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement. The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the Liberals to go into a coalition with One Nation.

In his speech in the dying minutes of the parliamentary term, Speakman, a member of the party’s moderate faction, warned the Liberals against becoming “Labor lite” or “One Nation lite”, saying they should stick to the values of “Menzian Liberalism”.

Referencing Pauline Hanson’s notion of “monoculture”, Speakman said Australia was “the most successful multicultural society on the planet” and was “so much better for it”.

“You know, we hear certain people say we want a monoculture, and that people who don’t support that monoculture somehow are enemies of Australia, hate Australia,” he said.

“I love Australia for its multiculturalism. Diversity is our strength. It is our strength, and we should build on that.”

Speakman, a barrister, served as minister for the environment between 2015 and 2017, and was attorney general between 2017 and the Perrottet government’s defeat in the 2023 election.

He was chosen as Liberal and opposition leader following Perrottet’s resignation, a position he held until November last year.

On Thursday, he said being opposition leader “is often said to be the toughest job in politics” and while it had “ultimately unravelled” for him, he had mostly led an opposition “which was competitive with, or even ahead of, the government in the polls”.

He said his record as attorney general included legislating for NSW to be the first Australian jurisdiction to criminalise coercive control, introducing affirmative consent tests in criminal sexual assault trials and reforming criminal and civil child sexual abuse cases.

Speakman’s resignation, ending speculation which bubbled up again when he spoke during question time on Thursday, is the latest blow for Sloane, who he said in his leaving speech had the “attributes to be a great premier”.

Earlier on Thursday, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, announced former Liberal councillor and parliamentary staffer Tanya Raffoul would contest the Liberal-held seat of Epping as a Labor candidate.

world.title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
world.snippet: The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits Environmentalists in South Afri...
world.content:
Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.

The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.

The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.

The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.

The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.

Otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”

Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, said she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted quickly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.

“As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.

The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.

Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.

“A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”

Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.

The trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”

Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.

The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” said Venter.

A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.

Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

world.title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
world.snippet: Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds One in four women around ...
world.content:
One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.

Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.

“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”

The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.

“The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.

He said that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.

In countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted, he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.

Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.

Alimatu Dimonekene, founder of A Girl At A Time, an organisation supporting adolescent girls in Sierra Leone, said a conversation around consent in marriage had yet to begin in Africa. “We’ve not even started the conversation [around marital rape],” she said. “Women will never call it rape; they make excuses for it or even blame themselves.”

She added: “In west Africa, sex is seen as an obligation in marriage. You must do whatever your husband demands.

“Once he has paid your bride price [a traditional marriage custom in which the bride’s family are paid money, livestock or goods by the groom], he owns you and you cannot reject his demands. Whatever he wants, he gets, including in terms of intimacy, finances and raising the children.”

world.title: Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling
world.snippet: A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza Fears are growing that the US could impose ...
world.content:
Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.

It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.

The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.

The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.

The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.

The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.

The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.

Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.

Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians.”

In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”

In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”

He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.

Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.

In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically”.

It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.

The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of The Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.

The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.

Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.

On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater willingness on the part of the US to abandon its plan to impose sanctions on the ICC.

world.title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
world.snippet: Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans The European Commission has been a...
world.content:
The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.

The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.

Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.

The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.

Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.

In confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.

If Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).

According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.

In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, said she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.

“The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik said. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”

Under the plan, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.

The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.

The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.

One of the EU conditions for Egypt to gain the first €1bn loan was to increase the number of Takaful and Karama beneficiary households by 100,000 to 4.7 million.

In a leaked report to lawmakers in the EU council of ministers and the European parliament, the commission described that requirement as “broadly fulfilled”.

The data in that report, however, reveals a net fall of 62,281 households during this period, owing to what the EU officials describe as “a multi-annual recertification process”. Some beneficiaries were added to the list but a larger number were removed because they were deemed ineligible.

In order to achieve a later instalment of €1.5bn, Egypt was required to “further expand” the programmes, adding 60,000 households to the Takaful and Karama beneficiaries list. A second leaked report to EU lawmakers shows that the commission concluded the target was “fulfilled” because 442,118 families were added to the list.

On this occasion, the commission did not report on numbers removed. Figures from Egypt’s ministry of social solidarity, however, show a net reduction of 23,453 beneficiaries to the programmes in the 11 months until June 2026, the period leading up to the release of that payment. The EU announced the release of the €1.5bn payment in July 2026.

The data has since been deleted from the Egyptian ministry website but the Guardian has seen screenshots and archived webpages.

During a period from 2024 to 26 when the EU required Egypt to add 160,000 households to the rolls of the Karama and Takaful programmes, there was a net decline of 85,734 households.

Timothy Kaldas, the deputy director of the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, said the commission had generally “done a poor job of leveraging the funds of European taxpayers to support genuine stabilisation” on the other side of the Mediterranean. “The strategic interest of Europe is seeing a more economically stable Egypt with a population that is less precarious,” he said.

Sandra Gómez López, a Spanish socialist MEP who recently visited Cairo to assess human rights in Egypt, said the data presented by the Guardian raised important questions. “The commission must explain transparently why it considers these commitments to have been fulfilled and demonstrate that European funding is genuinely contributing to improving social protection for the Egyptian population,” she said.

She stressed that the EU should not withdraw support, “but neither can we allow the country’s strategic importance to lead us to lower our standards when it comes to human rights”.

For critics, the questions about the EU’s willingness to hold Egypt accountable on very precise socioeconomic targets do not bode well for the broader but less defined goals for democracy and human rights.

Strik said: “The fact that Egypt and the commission even seem to ignore the crystal-clear socioeconomic conditions doesn’t increase my expectation that they adhere to the vague precondition on democracy and the rule of law.”

Claudio Francavilla, an associate EU director at Human Rights Watch, said: “Without benchmarks, the EU has turned a human rights conditionality into a blank cheque for Egypt’s authoritarianism.”

In a statement to the Guardian, the European Commission said the policy target on Takaful and Karama referred to new beneficiary families “and not to its net increase”. The spokesperson said there was “no contradiction” between this statement and that in a confidential document that said Egypt was required to “further expand cash transfer programmes”.

Asked about the release of the remaining €1.5bn in promised loans, the commission said it “will be made once all conditions have been met”, referring to 24 economic policy conditions, keeping an IMF programme on track and “taking concrete and credible steps towards respecting effective democratic mechanisms, including a multiparty parliamentary system, and the rule of law, and guaranteeing respect for human rights”.

It added: “Compliance with the conditionality is examined thoroughly” by EU officials and diplomats based on “information provided by the Egyptian authorities and other relevant sources”.

Egypt’s mission to the EU in Brussels did not respond to a request for comment.

world.title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
world.snippet: Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’ Five EU member ...
world.content:
Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.

In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.

Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.

In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.

Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.

The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.

The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.

Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.

The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”

Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”

Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.

Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, said on Monday the move had no “future or humanity”. “I don’t see any future or humanity in that. It’s not the solution,” Sanchez, an outspoken defender of immigration in a Europe that has tilted to the right in recent years, told Telecinco television.

The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”

Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.

“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.

Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.

Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.
